opus-5.5.text:
Before I started my own group, I had a fairly naive picture: the PI sits down, decides what the important problems are, and then hires students to go work on them. It's a very top-down model, and I think a lot of people coming out of a PhD carry some version of it around.

What I've learned is that it really doesn't work that way, and honestly I'm glad it doesn't. The agenda of a lab ends up being much more of a negotiation, and a lot of it is set by the students. People show up with their own interests, their own intuitions about what's exciting, and sometimes their own stubbornness about what they want to work on. Some of the best projects we've done started as something a student wanted to try that I was mildly skeptical about. My role turned out to be less "here's the problem" and more "here's a question that connects what you care about to what the rest of the group is thinking about."

So I've come to see my job as something closer to curation, or maybe gardening. I try to keep a few big-picture questions in view. For us that's been things like how language relates to the structure of the world, and what models actually represent internally. Then I help people find their own paths into those questions. I also try to make sure that projects talk to each other, so the lab is more than a collection of unrelated papers.

The other thing that changed is how much the agenda is shaped by the field around you. Especially over the last several years, things move so fast that you can't plan a five-year program the way you might have imagined. You have to keep some core commitments stable while staying flexible enough to notice when the ground has shifted. A big part of that responsiveness comes from students too, because they're often the ones who notice first that something new is worth paying attention to.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the lab’s agenda is negotiated and that much of it is set by students, connecting that point to the PI’s experience starting a group.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes helping students connect their interests to broader questions, but does not clearly characterize the PI as a sounding board for ideas independently generated by lab members.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss retrospective accounts or say they impose more structure on how a lab’s agenda actually evolves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's changed a lot. When I was a grad student, I had this picture that the PI was the person who decided what the lab worked on. You'd walk into the group meeting, the professor would say "here's the direction," and everyone would go execute on it. And I think when I started at MIT I sort of expected that would be my job, that I'd be the one holding the agenda in my head and handing out pieces of it.

What actually happened is that the agenda emerged much more bottom-up than I anticipated. The students I ended up with came in with their own interests, their own intuitions about what mattered, and the projects that have actually gone somewhere are mostly ones where a student came to me with something I wouldn't have thought to ask, and my role was to help sharpen it, connect it to something bigger, or tell them which version of the question was tractable. So I've gone from thinking of myself as the person who sets the direction to thinking of myself as something more like an editor, or maybe a curator. I decide who's in the room, I decide which questions I get excited about and push on, and that shapes things, but the ideas themselves are much more distributed than I expected.

The other thing I underestimated is how much the agenda gets set from outside the lab entirely. Funding agencies, what's happening in industry, what reviewers at NeurIPS or ACL are willing to accept this year. When I was a student that felt like background noise. As a PI you realize that those forces are constantly pulling on what's possible, and part of the job is figuring out when to push against them and when to ride them. In the last few years especially, with so much of the field's center of gravity moving to industry labs, a lot of the agenda-setting I do is really about asking: what's the question that a university lab is uniquely positioned to answer, that nobody with a giant compute budget is going to bother with? That wasn't a question I had to think about at all five or six years ago.

So the short version is: I thought it was one person's job, and it turns out it's a negotiation between the students, me, and a lot of forces none of us control.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that after starting at MIT, the agenda emerged bottom-up: students brought their own interests, and most successful projects began with a student’s idea.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes the PI’s role as sharpening student-generated ideas, connecting them to broader questions, and identifying tractable versions.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss retrospective accounts or say that they make the agenda’s evolution seem more structured than it was.

astra-6.text:
Before I became a PI, I think I imagined that the professor was the person who decided what the lab worked on: you had some vision, and then you recruited students to help execute it. And the experience has felt much more bottom-up than that. Students come in with their own interests, they discover something surprising, and that ends up pulling the whole group in a direction I wouldn’t have anticipated.

I still have a role in choosing which questions to encourage and helping connect individual projects to a bigger picture. And choosing whom to recruit is itself a big part of setting an agenda. But the agenda emerges from those interactions much more than it comes from me sitting down and writing out a five-year plan. A lot of the job is recognizing when a student has found something interesting and giving them room to pursue it.

r001.rationale: The response says students’ interests and discoveries can pull the group’s agenda, but it does not place this claim specifically at the start of a new lab.

r002.rationale: The PI is described as encouraging questions and giving students room to pursue discoveries, but not as a sounding board for ideas independently generated by lab members.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss retrospective accounts or whether they make the agenda’s evolution seem more structured than it was.

sol-6.1.text:
Before I became a PI, I think I imagined that the PI had a much more coherent plan: here are the questions we’re going to answer, and here’s how all the projects fit together. And certainly part of the job is to have some sense of which questions matter and where there might be opportunities to make progress. But the agenda is much more collaborative than that picture suggests.

Students come in with their own interests, and they notice things that I wouldn’t have noticed. A project takes an unexpected turn, and suddenly that opens up a direction that becomes a substantial part of what the group does. So a lot of my role is helping people develop those ideas, making connections between them, and figuring out when to encourage someone to keep pushing on something that isn’t working yet.

I still have questions that I’m excited about and try to get other people excited about. But my understanding of what the lab should be working on changes through those conversations. The students are shaping my research agenda at least as much as I’m shaping theirs.

r001.rationale: The response says students shape the agenda, but does not say they set it when a PI is starting a new lab.

r002.rationale: It describes the PI as helping develop students’ own ideas, making connections, and encouraging them to keep pursuing work—an equivalent role to a sounding board for lab members’ ideas.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts an imagined coherent plan with a collaborative process, but says nothing about retrospective accounts imposing too much structure on how the agenda evolved.
